PaidHR ’s launch of Vuzo is a quietly significant move for African HR tech.

Most payroll startups chase direct customers one business at a time — a slow, capital-intensive way to scale across markets like Nigeria, where the vast majority of businesses are informal, fragmented, and hard to reach through traditional sales. By unbundling its payroll engine into embeddable infrastructure, PaidHR founded by Seye Bandele and Lekan Omotosho is making a deliberate bet: distribution over acquisition. Instead of fighting for every customer directly, let fintechs, HR platforms, neobanks, and vertical SaaS tools plug payroll into what they’ve already built.

This mirrors a pattern that’s played out repeatedly in global fintech — Stripe didn’t win by acquiring every merchant, it won by becoming the layer every other product quietly ran on. Unit did something similar for banking-as-a-service. The pattern works because the hard, unglamorous part that is compliance, tax calculation, pension remittance, statutory filings that differ across jurisdictions becomes someone else’s problem to solve once, and everyone else’s problem to never solve at all. That’s a real moat, because getting payroll compliance wrong in Africa’s patchwork of regulatory environments isn’t a minor bug, it’s a legal and financial liability for whoever owns the customer relationship.

What makes this notable isn’t just the product decision, it’s the implicit admission in the announcement itself: “we can’t acquire all the customers in Africa.” That’s an unusually honest read of market reality from a founder, and it reframes PaidHR’s ambition. They’re no longer trying to be the payroll app for every business; they’re trying to be the infrastructure underneath every app that touches payroll.

If Vuzo executes well, PaidHR’s growth stops being bottlenecked by its own sales capacity and starts compounding with every platform that integrates it, a much steeper curve than direct-to-business SaaS typically allows. The open question is adoption speed: how quickly platforms with payroll-adjacent customers (think fintechs, ERP tools, gig-economy platforms) decide it’s cheaper to embed than to build. Worth watching closely over the next year.

PaidHR analysed payroll records for more than 25,000 workers across over 400 Nigerian employers, using a July 2026 snapshot of active employees on its platform.

The report puts the median monthly gross salary at ₦217,000 ($163), with workers taking home ₦199,972 ($150) after deductions.

Workers with less than a year at their current job earn a median salary of ₦181,235 ($136.28). Pay rises with tenure and peaks around the five-year mark, when the middle worker earns about 47% more than someone at entry level. After that, the gains become much less consistent.

How do you decide what a role is worth?

When hiring, setting a salary can mean balancing several things: the company’s budget, industry benchmarks, the candidate’s expectations and what the previous person in the role earned.

But which of these actually drives the final decision?
We put this question to HR leaders and business owners in our community, and the responses got us thinking about how organisations approach compensation.

While budgets and internal salary structures matter, relying on them alone may leave employers without a clear picture of what the market currently pays for a role.

Salary benchmarks provide useful context. They help organisations assess whether their offers are competitive, set more informed salary ranges and have better-grounded compensation conversations with prospective employees.

This is one of the reasons we created PaidRight: to bring more visibility to salary data and help people better understand where they stand across roles and salary brackets.
Because compensation decisions shouldn't be based on guesswork alone. They should be informed by data.

Explore the PaidRight report and get a clearer picture of the salary landscape.

To my first customers “our employees”. 💙
Last week was Customer Experience Week, and honestly, it was a very busy week for us.

I had a training at ICS Outsourcing Nigeria Limited , one of my team members was ill, and we still had to pull everything together from the HR desk.

We wanted to do something special for the team, and we decided Friday was going to be the day.

So tell me why I found myself in the office at almost midnight with decorators. Going the extra mile, literally!

We were transforming the office so that when everyone walked in the next morning, they would have a little surprise waiting for them.Friday came, and seeing everyone walk in, take pictures, enjoy the space, and just have a good time made it worth it.

We also curated gifts for the team, had my friend Goodness Goodness "Ada" Armstrong (CIPD) join us for a conversation about customer experience and career growth, and spent time talking about what it means to go the extra mile.

In HR, we talk a lot about employee experience. But sometimes, you have to actually create the moments people get to experience.

It doesn't always have to be a big thing. Sometimes, it's the thought, the effort, and the fact that somebody took the time to make you feel considered.

Anyway, this was our Customer Experience Week at PaidHR.

And yes, HR was outside. Literally. At midnight.

PS: It’s a mini Vlog, grab your popcorn 😉
